candidates.attacker_control: The `Map` parameters passed to `RepositoryFactory.getRepository(Map)` (and to `JcrUtils.getRepository(Map/String)`), typically derived from an application-supplied repository URI or configuration: the attacker controls the `org.apache.jackrabbit.repository.jndi.name` value or the `jndi:` URI, including its authority, and thus the JNDI provider/context factory and lookup target. In the secondary paths, the `Context`/`name` (JNDIRepositoryFactory) or the repository binding name (RegistryHelper) are supplied by the application using the API.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Critical counterevidence: in this snapshot the lookup is disabled unless the system property `jackrabbit.jndi.enabled` is set (JndiRepositoryFactory line 62; JNDIRepositoryFactory line 65; RegistryHelper lines 64/100), and `JndiRepositoryFactory.getRepository` returns null without looking anything up, so a default build is not exploitable via this path. I confirmed the gate is applied consistently to the generic factory, the deprecated factory and the bind/unbind helper, and that the only other JNDI lookups in the tree (`ConnectionFactory`, `JNDIRepositoryServlet`, `JNDIBindingServlet`, `JNDIDatabaseJournal`/`JNDIDatabasePersistenceManager`) use names taken from repository/servlet configuration rather than remote request data. No runtime testing was performed; exploitability above the flag was not verified.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution (or at least attacker-directed class loading / deserialization) in the process that resolves the JCR repository, as well as SSRF-style access to internal JNDI services, when JNDI lookups are enabled and the repository parameters come from an untrusted source. If treated as the historical JCR-5135 issue, this is the code location the project disabled by default to remove the RCE exposure.
candidates.prerequisites: JNDI must be enabled: `-Djackrabbit.jndi.enabled=true` (JCR-5135 made this non-default) — lines 62/72 of JndiRepositoryFactory, line 65 of JNDIRepositoryFactory, lines 64/100 of RegistryHelper. The application must pass untrusted values into the repository lookup (URI or parameter map). A reachable malicious LDAP/RMI/other JNDI provider must be resolvable by the client, and the target JVM must be able to deserialize/load the returned object (typical pre-JDK 8u191 or permissive `trustURLCodebase` settings, or any gadget/`ObjectFactory` on the classpath).
candidates.root_cause: `JndiRepositoryFactory.getRepository(Map)` converts caller-supplied repository settings directly into a JNDI environment and lookup: any `org.apache.jackrabbit.repository.jndi.name` value becomes the JNDI name, and for a `jndi:` repository URI the URI authority is copied verbatim into `Context.INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY` (line 115). `getRepository(name, environment)` then executes `new InitialContext(environment).lookup(name)` (line 124). Because both the context factory and the lookup name are attacker-influenceable, a crafted value (e.g. an LDAP/RMI URL) causes the JVM to resolve a remote context and load/execute remote classes (RemoteObject factory / codebase), i.e. RCE in the process that resolves the repository. The same sink exists in `org.apache.jackrabbit.commons.repository.JNDIRepositoryFactory.getRepository()` (line 67) and in `RegistryHelper.unregisterRepository()` (line 101, `ctx.lookup(name)`), all three of which are gated by the shared `JNDI_ENABLED` constant. The source documents this history: `JndiRepositoryFactory` line 60 says "Disabled by default, see JCR-5135".
candidates.title: Untrusted repository parameters drive JNDI lookup in JndiRepositoryFactory (JNDI injection; mitigated by disabled-by-default JCR-5135 gate)
candidates.trace: Untrusted repository URI/parameter -> `JcrUtils.getRepository(Map)`/`JcrUtils.REPOSITORY_URI` -> `JndiRepositoryFactory.getRepository(Map)` (line 70) -> `new URI(...)` parsed, scheme `jndi` -> `getRepository(uri, environment)` (line 100) -> `environment.put(Context.INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY, authority)` (line 115) -> `new InitialContext(environment).lookup(name)` (line 124) -> remote context resolves and returns the repository object, loading attacker-directed classes. Parallel: `JNDIRepositoryFactory.getRepository()` line 67 `context.lookup(name)`; `RegistryHelper.unregisterRepository` line 101 `ctx.lookup(name)`.
candidates.unverified: Whether any deployment in scope re-enables `jackrabbit.jndi.enabled`, and whether this snapshot is the pre-fix state of a different security change (the snapshot already contains the JCR-5135 gate, so I could not prove the snapshot precedes a specific unfixed vulnerability). The JNDI provider used, class-loading restrictions in the target JVM, and the concrete gadget chain were not executed or validated.
candidates.weakness_type: JNDI injection / code injection via untrusted lookup name and context environment (CWE-94-class, related to CWE-502/unsafe JNDI usage)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot (2,064 model-visible files: all 18 modules' `src/main` Java/resources plus build/webapp files; the snapshot contains no test sources, so no test-based signals were available). Work was source-only: full file listing and text search across the tree, then targeted reading of the security-critical paths — jackrabbit-jcr-commons (`JndiRepositoryFactory`, `JNDIRepositoryFactory`, `JcrUtils`, XML/JSON helpers), jackrabbit-core (JNDI helpers, authentication/token, ACL/user management, node type XML, persistence/data store, WebDAV-free core session), jackrabbit-webdav (request parsing, CSRF, servlet dispatch, XML factory), jackrabbit-jcr-server (remoting servlet/diff handling, WebDAV resources, import handlers), jackrabbit-spi-commons/spi2dav (parsers, ExceptionConverter, HTTP/TLS setup), jackrabbit-webapp (servlets/JSPs), and jackrabbit-data (FileSystem/DataStore). Line-level reads were performed on the strongest candidates and their callers; all other files were searched systematically for dangerous sinks (exec, deserialization, Class.forName/newInstance, JNDI, XML factories, SQL/statement construction, file/path building, random/crypto, permission checks).
limitations: No code was compiled, executed, or dynamically tested; all conclusions are static and could not be runtime-confirmed.
The snapshot contains only main sources and resources (no tests, no git history, no build artifacts), so recently changed lines and the corresponding fix/test cannot be identified directly.

The repository version (2.23.2-beta-SNAPSHOT) already contains the JCR-5135 JNDI mitigation (and other historical fixes such as JCR-3174/CSRF hardening), so I could not rule out that this case concerns a later, not-yet-visible fix in a file I could not single out.
Dependency code (e.g., Apache HttpClient, Tika, Lucene, Derby) is not present in the snapshot and was not audited.

Exploitability of the JNDI candidate depends on deployment configuration (`jackrabbit.jndi.enabled`), the JNDI provider available at runtime, and JDK class-loading restrictions, none of which can be verified from source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: `jackrabbit-spi2dav` ExceptionConverter instantiates classes named by the WebDAV server's error XML (`Class.forName(getChildText(exc,"class")).getConstructor(String.class).newInstance(msg)`, lines 61-80): a malicious/compromised server can force construction of arbitrary `(String)`-constructor classes on the client (e.g. FileWriter/FileOutputStream side effects).
rejected_leads.reason: Real unsafe-reflection pattern, but the code is long-standing (references JCR-2536, 2007), only reachable client-side from a server-supplied error body, and I found no fix marker or advisory tie in the snapshot; impact depends on gadget classes and is weaker/more speculative than the JNDI sink.

rejected_leads.lead: XML parsing without entity-resolution/DTD restrictions: `DOMWalker`/`NodeTypeReader` (jackrabbit-core, lines 40-67/57-60) and `PrivilegeXmlHandler` (spi-commons, lines 110-116, used by `AbstractRecord.readPrivilegeDef`) create DocumentBuilderFactories without disabling external entities.
rejected_leads.reason: XXE pattern is real, but reachable only through privileged node-type registration/local nodetype files, local privilege XML, or cluster-journal records (trusted shared storage); no remote, low-privileged path was identified in the snapshot, so it does not meet the top-candidate bar.

rejected_leads.lead: Java deserialization sinks: `SessionInfoImpl.duplicateCredentials` round-trips `Credentials` through ObjectInputStream, and `AsyncUploadCache` reads maps/sets via ObjectInputStream from local files.
rejected_leads.reason: The serialized data is self-produced (credentials that the application already created) or read from local data-store files, not from remote/untrusted input; no attacker-controlled stream could be traced.

rejected_leads.lead: Path handling in `LocalFileSystem`, `FSDirectoryManager`, `FileDataStore`/`CachingDataStore` (`new File(root, name)`, 2/4/6-char `substring` on identifiers).
rejected_leads.reason: Names are internal (index names, digest-derived identifiers) or MAC-validated in `AbstractDataStore.getRecordFromReference`; the `substring` assumptions can only yield an exception (local DoS), not a traversal, for the reachable inputs I traced.

rejected_leads.lead: WebDAV request handling oddities: `WebdavRequestImpl.getMemberLocator` string concatenation, `AbstractLocatorFactory` path handling, `AbstractWebdavServlet` continuing after a 415 content-coding rejection, `CSRFUtil` log message claiming protection is disabled on the enabled default path.
rejected_leads.reason: JCR path validation rejects traversal in the repository layer, the 415 branch is unreachable for requests created by `AbstractWebdavServlet` (WebdavRequestImpl implements ContentCodingAwareRequest), and the CSRF mismatch is a log-text defect with protection still enabled — no security impact established.

summary: Source-only review of the Apache Jackrabbit trunk snapshot (all 18 modules, 2,064 files, main sources/resources only — no tests). I traced the remote/parameter-driven input paths (WebDAV request handling, JCR remoting, XML import/parsing, user/ACL administration, data-store and persistence file handling) and the most recent security-relevant change markers in the tree. The strongest distinct candidate is the JNDI lookup in `jackrabbit-jcr-commons`' `JndiRepositoryFactory` (with the same pattern in `repository/JNDIRepositoryFactory` and `jackrabbit-core`'s `RegistryHelper`): caller-supplied repository parameters / a `jndi:` repository URI control both the JNDI name and, via the URI authority, `Context.INITIAL_CONTEXT_FACTORY`, and are passed to `new InitialContext(environment).lookup(name)` — the classic JNDI-injection/RCE sink that the source itself documents as the reason for the `JCR-5135` mitigation (`JNDI_ENABLED`, disabled by default). Counterevidence is important: in this exact snapshot the lookup is gated behind `-Djackrabbit.jndi.enabled=true`, so it is not exploitable in a default deployment; I therefore report it as a lead (medium confidence), not a confirmed vulnerability. I found no other enabled, demonstrably exploitable flaw of comparable severity in the inspected code.
